title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Overview

We quantify linear relationships between a response variable (dependent) and explanatory variables (independent variables or predictors) using simple and multiple linear regression models.
Linear models (LMs) are relatively simple, but incredibly powerful

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Simulate data
We will use (made-up) plant data to illustrate how simple linear regression models are fitted. First, we clear the workspace and simulate three datasets.

set.seed(541)
# data1: intercept-only (plant heights)
data1 <- data.frame(id        = paste0("A", 1:100),
                    height_cm = rnorm(100, mean = 23.09, sd = 2.82))
# data2: height ~ nitrogen
data2 <- data.frame(id             = paste0("A", 1:100),
                    nitrogen_gsqm  = runif(100, 50, 700),
                    height_cm      = NA)
data2$height_cm <- 23.15 + 0.00985 * data2$nitrogen_gsqm + rnorm(100, 0, 2.84)
# data3: height ~ species (A vs B)
data3 <- data.frame(id      = paste0("plant", 1:100),
                    species = rep(c("Species A", "Species B"), 50))
data3$height_cm <- ifelse(data3$species == "Species A",
                          rnorm(50, 23.53, 2.8),
                          rnorm(50, 20.17, 2.8))


These data consist of the individual identification (id) and height (in cm) of 100 plants. All heights were measured 30 days after germination.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Intercept-only model
The height of the plants is our variable of interest and we can fit a simple linear regression model using the lm() function. You can specify an intercept-only model by using a “1” after the tilde (∼) in the regression formula.

library(stats)
m1 <- stats::lm(height_cm ~ 1, data = data1)
summary(m1)







Note



We have a response variable (height_cm), but no predictor variables. Therefore, we cannot estimate a slope, only an intercept term. In the absence of a slope, the intercept is equivalent to the mean height of all plants.








Tip



The model output can be displayed with the summary() function.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Intercept-only model
The intercept value is the average height (in cm) of plants in this sample. The low p-value indicates that this value is significantly different from 0. Next, let’s plot the data and add the regression line.

plot(data1$height_cm,
     pch = 19, 
     col = "grey",
     ylab = "Plant height (cm)")
abline(m1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Intercept-only model
To better understand what residuals are, let’s add them to the plot as well. To do so, we obtain the model-predicted value for each data point (i.e., the height a plant would have had if it were on the regression line) using the predict() function. Then we just connect each data point with its predicted value using segments().

plot(data1$height_cm,
     pch = 19,
     col = "grey",
     ylab = "Plant height (cm)")
abline(m1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
fit <- predict(m1)
segments(seq_along(data1$height_cm),
         fit,
         seq_along(data1$height_cm),
         data1$height_cm)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Intercept-only model
Plotting a scatter plot or a regression line is not that useful when dealing with an intercept-only model. As an alternative, we can plot the density distribution of the data (the response variable) and then superimpose both the calculated and model-estimated mean. And as we just mentioned, these are identical.

plot(density(data1$height_cm))
abline(v = mean(data1$height_cm), lwd = 6, col = grey(0.4))  # calculated mean
abline(v = coef(m1), lwd = 2, col = "orange")   # model estimated mean

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous predictor
Generally, in regression analysis, we are interested in quantifying the relationship between predictor and response variables. We now inspect data2, which, in addition to each plant’s height, also contains the amount of Nitrogen added to each plant’s growing soil (g per \(m^2\)). First, we inspect the data and visualize plant height against nitrogen addition:

head(data2)
plot(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm,
     data = data2,
     pch = 19,
     col = "grey",
     xlab = expression(Nitrogen~addition~(g/m^2)),
     ylab = "Plant height (cm)")







Tip



Always include units with axes labels.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous predictor
We can fit a linear regression model to the data; this model includes a slope term for the effect of soil nitrogen concentration on plant height. The intercept term is implied and does not need to be specified in the formula.

m2 <- stats::lm(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = data2)
summary(m2)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous predictor
The intercept (23.15 cm) is the expected height of a plant when the nitrogen added to the soil is 0 g /\(m^2\). The slope coefficient (0.0099 cm) is the expected increase in plant height in cm for every 1 g /\(m^2\) increase in nitrogen added to the soil. The low p-value indicates that this slope is significantly different from 0.

How would you summarize this finding?


One way to summarize this finding could be: We detected a significant positive relationship between plant height and the amount of nitrogen added to the soil (beta = 0.01, t = 8.11, p <0.001). For example, a plant supplemented with 100 g soil nitrogen reached an average height of 24.14 cm compared with 23.15 cm for a plant without supplementary nitrogen.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous predictor
We can use the model object to add the regression line to the scatter plot. And as earlier, we can also show the residuals in the same plot.

plot(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm, 
     data = data2,
     pch = 19,
     col = "grey",
     xlab = "Nitrogen addition (g/m^2)",
     ylab = "Plant height (cm)")
abline(m2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
fit <- predict(m2)
segments(data2$nitrogen_gsqm,
         fit,
         data2$nitrogen_gsqm,
         data2$height_cm)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical predictor
We can also use categorical predictor variables. In a linear regression, such variables are dealt with by turning them into so-called dummy variables. This is done by setting one level as a reference value (set to 0; this is the one associated with the intercept). All other levels (set to 1) are then compared with the reference level, one by one. We illustrate the use of categorical predictors in simple linear regression using a new version of the plant data.

head(data3)



This data set contains the id and height for two species of plants (species A and B).

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical predictor
Next, we fit the simple linear regression with species as the predictor variable:

m3 <- stats::lm(height_cm ~ species, data = data3)
summary(m3)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical predictor
The intercept (23.53 cm) is the expected height of a plant of the reference species (A). The slope coefficient (-3.36 cm) is the expected difference in plant height of species B compared with species A. The negative coefficient indicates that the height of species B is (on average) lower than the height of species A. The low p-value indicates that the difference is significant. >How would you summarize this finding?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical predictor
One way to summarize this finding could be: Species A grew significantly higher than species B (beta = -3.36, t = -5.991, p <0.001). The average height following a 30-day growing period for species A was 23.53 cm, compared with 20.17 cm for species B.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical predictor
Finally, we plot the data and add the regression line:

boxplot(height_cm ~ species,
        data = data3,
        at = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "",
        ylab = "Plant height (cm)")
abline(m3, col = "red", lwd = 2)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Overview
Regression models can have multiple predictors. This lesson will give you a basic understanding of the effects estimates (coefficients) generated by multiple linear regression. When the effects of multiple predictor variables in a regression are independent of each other, we refer to them as additive effects. Today, we look at three examples with different predictor variables that have additive effects on the response.

p1 <- data.frame(id        = paste0("P", 1:100),
                 species   = rep(c("Species A", "Species B"), 50),
                 pesticide = rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), each = 50),
                 height_cm = NA) # Plant Data 1: species + pesticide (categorical + categorical)
p1$height_cm <- 23.5 +
                ifelse(p1$species == "Species B", -3.4, 0) +
                ifelse(p1$pesticide, 2.1, 0) +
                rnorm(100, 0, 2.5)
p2 <- data.frame(nitrogen_gsqm = runif(100, 50, 700),
                 species       = rep(c("Species A", "Species B"), 50),
                 height_cm     = NA) # Plant Data 2: nitrogen + species (continuous + categorical)
p2$height_cm <- 22 +
                0.01 * p2$nitrogen_gsqm +
                ifelse(p2$species == "Species B", -3.0, 0) +
                rnorm(100, 0, 2.5)
p3 <- data.frame( nitrogen_gsqm = runif(100, 50, 700),
                  temperature   = rep(c(15, 25), 50),
                  height_cm     = NA) # Plant Data 3: nitrogen + temperature (continuous + continuous)
p3$height_cm <- 20 +
                0.01 * p3$nitrogen_gsqm +
                0.5  * p3$temperature +
                rnorm(100, 0, 2.5)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical + Categorical
We fit a linear regression model to the first data object. This regression model contains the additive effects of species (Species A and Species B) and whether pesticide was applied during the growth period (TRUE/FALSE).

m1 <- stats::lm(height_cm ~ species + pesticide, data = p1)
summary(m1)







Note



The output contains separate coefficients for the intercept and every effect included in the model. Remember, categorical variables are treated as dummy variables, with one category serving as the intercept value (0) to which each additional category is then compared.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical + Categorical
The model object essentially contains a machine that can be used to make predictions, i.e., to calculate the expected value of the response variable (height_cm) given certain values of the predictor variables (species and pesticide).
To make a prediction, we first create a new data object (in this case, one that contains all possible combinations of species and pesticide). We then provide that data object to the predict() function which generates the predictions (fitted values of plant height) for each set of predictor values, as well as the associated standard errors.

new_data <- expand.grid(species   = c("Species A", "Species B"),
                        pesticide = c(FALSE, TRUE))
temp <- predict(m1, newdata = new_data, se.fit = TRUE)
new_data$fit    <- temp$fit
new_data$uci    <- new_data$fit + 1.96 * temp$se.fit
new_data$lci    <- new_data$fit - 1.96 * temp$se.fit

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Categorical + Categorical
We can use what you have previously learned about plotting in R to generate a graph that visualizes the results (model predictions).

cols <- c("orange", "turquoise")
names(cols) <- sort(unique(new_data$species))

plot(fit ~ as.numeric(pesticide),
     data = new_data,
     xlim = c(-0.25, 1.25),
     col  = cols[species],
     pch = 19,
     cex = 2,
     ylim = c(min(new_data$lci), max(new_data$uci)),
     axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Treatment",
     ylab = "Height (cm)")
axis(1, at = c(0, 1), labels = c("w/o pesticide", "w/ pesticide"))
axis(2)
# Add confidence intervals
segments(as.numeric(new_data$pesticide),
         new_data$lci,
         as.numeric(new_data$pesticide),
         new_data$uci,
         col  = cols[new_data$species],
         lwd  = 5,
         lend = 1)
# Add legend
legend("topleft", 
       legend = names(cols), 
       pch    = 19,
       pt.cex = 2,
       col    = cols, 
       bty    = "n")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous + Categorical
Let’s fit a model with one continuous and one categorical predictor variable.

m2 <- stats::lm(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm + species, data = p2)
summary(m2)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous + Categorical
Then create a new table with combination of predictor variables and use the predict ():

n_range  <- seq(min(p2$nitrogen_gsqm),
                max(p2$nitrogen_gsqm),
                length.out = 50)
new_data <- expand.grid(nitrogen_gsqm = n_range,
                        species       = c("Species A", "Species B"))
temp <- predict(m2, newdata = new_data, se.fit = TRUE)
new_data$fit <- temp$fit
new_data$uci <- new_data$fit + 1.96 * temp$se.fit
new_data$lci <- new_data$fit - 1.96 * temp$se.fit

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous + Categorical
Finally, plot the results:

cols <- c("orange", "turquoise")
names(cols) <- sort(unique(new_data$species))

plot(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm,
     data = p2,
     pch = 19,
     col = cols[species],
     cex = 0.4,
     ylab = "Height (cm)",
     xlab = "Nitrogen (g/m²)")
for (sp in names(cols)) {
  sub <- new_data[new_data$species == sp, ]
  # Add regression line
  lines(fit ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = sub, col = cols[sp], lwd = 3)
  # Add confidence intervals
  lines(lci ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = sub, col = cols[sp], lty = 2)
  lines(uci ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = sub, col = cols[sp], lty = 2)
}
# Add legend
legend("topleft", 
       legend = names(cols),
       lwd    = 3, 
       col    = cols,
       bty    = "n", 
       title  = "Species")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous + Continuous
Let’s fit a model with two continuous predictor variables.

m3 <- stats::lm(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm + temperature, data = p3)
summary(m3)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Continuous + Continuous
We can make predictions and visualize the results as before.

n_range  <- seq(min(p3$nitrogen_gsqm),
                max(p3$nitrogen_gsqm),
                length.out = 50)
new_data <- expand.grid(nitrogen_gsqm = n_range,
                        temperature   = c(15, 25))
temp <- predict(m3, newdata = new_data, se.fit = TRUE)
new_data$fit <- temp$fit
new_data$uci <- new_data$fit + 1.96 * temp$se.fit
new_data$lci <- new_data$fit - 1.96 * temp$se.fit

cols  <- c("orange", "turquoise")
cats  <- sort(unique(new_data$temperature))
names(cols) <- as.character(cats)
plot(height_cm ~ nitrogen_gsqm,
     data = p3,
     pch = 19,
     cex = 0.4,
     ylab = "Height (cm)", xlab = "Nitrogen (g/m²)")

for (t in as.character(cats)) {
  sub <- new_data[as.character(new_data$temperature) == t, ]
  #Add regression line
  lines(fit ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = sub, col = cols[t], lwd = 3)
  #Add confidence intervals
  lines(lci ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = sub, col = cols[t], lty = 2)
  lines(uci ~ nitrogen_gsqm, data = sub, col = cols[t], lty = 2)
}
#Add legend
legend("topleft",
       legend = paste(cats, "°C"),
       lwd = 3, 
       col = cols,
       bty = "n",
       title = "Temperature")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
R Syntax
A core component in R is the object. Objects can contain almost anything: data, models, and functions.

# Assign a sequence of numbers to object x
x <- 1:15

# Display it
print(x)



Objects can contain almost anything, including data, statistical models, and functions. Here you will get an introduction to creating and working with simple data objects. For example, we assigned a series of numbers to an object named “x”.


By typing the name of the object and executing that line (with Ctrl+R or Ctrl+Enter), we can get R to display the current contents of a given object. Alternatively, you can use the print() function.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
R Syntax
You can assign the result of a calculation to an object:

x <- 1 + 15

y <- 5.2          # second object

z <- x ^ y        # third object



Notice how x now contains the new value; the previous content has been overwritten.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
R Syntax
How do you find all objects you’ve created?

x <- 1 + 15
y <- 5.2
z <- x ^ y

ls()              # lists objects in the workspace


You can use objects as you would the value they contain. For example, we can create another object with the value 5.2 and then combine x and y in a calculation with the result assigned to z.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
R Syntax
Objects can also contain other types of information, including strings and boolean characters (TRUE/FALSE). Objects may contain only a single value, e.g., objects x and y. But objects can contain much more, including entire data sets. You will learn about additional types of variables later.

x <- "leopard"
y <- FALSE

class(x)
class(y)







Note



String variables are surrounded by quotation marks; TRUE / FALSE are not.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
R Syntax: vectors
A vector is a sequence of values. Use c() to combine values:

# Numeric vector
mass_kg <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)

# Character vector
species <- c("leopard", "bear", "fox", "wolf")

# Logical vector
us_range <- c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
R Syntax: dataframes
A dataframe stitches vectors together as columns of a table:

mass_kg  <- c(38, 217, 7, 40)
species  <- c("leopard", "bear", "fox", "wolf")
us_range <- c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)

sp_data <- data.frame(species, mass_kg, us_range)
sp_data

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Snapshot USA
Snapshot USA is a coordinated monitoring of mammals (and birds) via camera traps across the US.
Today we explore a subset of this processed dataset.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Overview
To analyze data, you need to get them into the R workspace. Typically, this means loading data from external files (e.g., .txt or .csv) and assigning them to an object. Eventually, you may also want to export an R data object to an external file, for example, after creating or processing data in R. There are numerous alternatives for loading and exporting data; next are just a few examples.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Loading data
First, let’s empty the workspace, in case there are objects from a previous analysis, which could interfere with what we are going to do now:

# Clear workspace
rm(list = ls())

Make sure the required R packages (also called libraries) are installed and loaded. In this example, we can use the ”readr” or ”utils” package to load our .csv file. Then, download the input file and make sure it is in the current working directory, and load it into R as shown below.

# Load the snapshot_usa dataset from GitHub
library(utils)
url_remote <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
path_git   <- "MTourani/WILD541_F2026/refs/heads/main/"
file_name  <- "snapshot_usa.csv"

snapshot_usa <- utils::read.csv(paste0(url_remote, path_git, file_name))

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Explore data
You can check that the file has been loaded correctly by displaying the entire object or, if it is too unwieldy, the first 6 rows with function head():



Each row = one observation
Each column = one variable



head(snapshot_usa)









Tip



What do you think the function tail() does?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Explore data
This object contains a data frame, which has two dimensions (rows and columns).

# How many rows and columns?
dim(snapshot_usa)
nrow(snapshot_usa)
ncol(snapshot_usa)


Function dim() returns the size of each dimension (number of rows and number of columns).

Both rows and columns can be named; dimnames() returns these names.

# How many rows and columns?
dimnames(snapshot_usa)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Explore data
You can also specify which rows you want shown by providing the row index in square brackets.

# Return rows 1 through 3
snapshot_usa[1:3, ]

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Explore data
You may only want to inspect a certain column in a data frame. Here are different ways to have R return a column of a data frame:

# Three ways to access a column
snapshot_usa$Species_Name         # by name with $
snapshot_usa[, "Species_Name"]    # by name with []
snapshot_usa[, 3]                 # by index







Tip



R is case sensitive and the lower/upper case should match the exact column name.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Quantitative summaries
We used summary() in previous class. Similarly, we can use functions mean(), median(), sd() to get summaries of any dataset.
For example, we can find the mean number of animals in the camera trap images using mean() and use round() to show whole numbers.

mean(snapshot_usa$Count)
round(mean(snapshot_usa$Count), 0)







Warning



Why won’t mean(snapshot_usa$Species_Name) work?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Sort and order
You may want to inspect a sorted column, or find the lowest or highest value in your data frame.

# Sort a column by spa
head(sort(snapshot_usa$Species_Name))

# Reorder the whole dataframe alphabetically by species
snapshot_usa[order(snapshot_usa$Species_Name), ]

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Getting help
If you are unsure about how to use a function, you can get help from R’s help facilities. For example, if you know the name of a function you can get the associated help pages displayed simply by typing “?” followed by the name of the function (e.g., ?order). If you are not sure about the function name, you can do a “fuzzy” search using “??” followed by the word that you are looking for.

?order          # help for a specific function
??aggregate     # fuzzy search

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Tallies
The function table() is a simple way to tally your data. For example, you can get the number of images per age class like this:

table(snapshot_usa$Age)


More complex tallies can also be obtained, for example the number of observations associated with the different combinations of “Age” and “Class”.

table(snapshot_usa$Age, snapshot_usa$Class)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Tallies
The function table() only counts the number of observations associated with different combinations of variables. We can use aggregate() if we want elements in a given category summarized differently. For example, we can calculate the mean number of animals in the camera trap images by age class:

# Mean count by age class
aggregate(Count ~ Age, data = snapshot_usa, FUN = mean)

By adding additional variables on the right side of the formula, we can break things down further:

# Break down further by species
head(aggregate(Count ~ Age + Species_Name,
               data = snapshot_usa, FUN = mean))

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Export data
You can take the modified data frame and export it as a comma-delimited text file that can then be opened with other software.

# Export as CSV
utils::write.csv(snapshot_usa, "snapshot_usa.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Export as RData
save(snapshot_usa, file = "snapshot_usa.RData")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Reload and inspect
Exporting your data as an R data file ensures that all information is stored and can be retrieved exactly the way it was when you last worked with it in R. You can confirm this by removing the object from the workspace and then loading the .RData file.

rm(snapshot_usa)           # remove from workspace

load("snapshot_usa.RData") # reload
head(snapshot_usa)

text:
Step 1: Understand Before You Prompt

Know your question and your data before you open the chat window.
Separate two different jobs: deciding what the analysis should do (your job) from typing the syntax (AI can help with this job).
Use AI to learn field conventions and relevant tools, not only to generate the final answer.
Sanity check: could you defend this line of code to your committee?







Warning


Watch out for vibe coding: accepting AI output you cannot evaluate, debug, or explain yourself.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab

Tool
Best for




Conversational (Claude, ChatGPT)
Architecture questions, debugging, learning a new package


IDE assistant (Copilot-style)
Autocompletion, staying in flow


Autonomous agent (Claude Code, Cursor)
Multi-file edits, rapid prototyping









Important



Check university guidelines for approved AI tools
Check AI model comparisons
Restate key constraints in long sessions as most tools don’t remember perfectly
Commit working code before a big AI-driven change, so you can always roll back

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Step 3: Test Everything, Trust Nothing

Ask for tests before or during implementation.
Verify the test outputs.
Verify the results against something you understand, e.g., a plot or summary statistics.







Note


Despite AI doesn’t know your data, i.e., if samples are paired, clustered, or spatially autocorrelated unless you tell it, it will still confidently hand you a test.
If the code ran without errors, it does not mean it is correct.

text:
Step 4: You Are Still the Scientist

The responsibility for AI-assisted code always belongs to the person who submits it.
“The AI wrote it” is not a defense for a mis-specified model, or results nobody else can reproduce.







Important


Rule of thumb: if you can’t explain a line at your defense, don’t turn it in

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Privacy & data sharing

Never paste into a public AI tool: unpublished results, embargoed or data subject to data-sharing agreement.
Data from Tribal lands, communities, or partnerships: additional authorization applies, regardless of a public tool’s terms of service
Precise locations of sensitive, threatened, or poaching-vulnerable species are often legally restricted and the coordinates should be treated as any other confidential data.
When unsure: troubleshoot with a simulated or anonymized subset, and ask before uploading anything real







Important


If you can’t anonymize data meaningfully, don’t paste it into a public AI tool.

Every university policy agrees on disclosing AI use.

Do vs Don’t
✔ Ask it to explain an error or an unfamiliar function
✔ Use it to learn a new package syntax
✔ Get a first draft of code structure

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Overview
There are many options and different criteria for model comparison. Here, we show a few popular methods in ecological research. Remember, all things equal, the simpler model is preferred over any more complex alternative. This is known as the ”principle of parsimony”.
The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) allows for model comparison and selection considering both the fit of the model (rewarded) and the number of parameters estimated (penalized). Here, we will use AIC-based selection methods to identify the top model in a set of candidate models.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Getting started
In a telemetry study, wolverines (Gulo gulo) were monitored to determine factors influencing survival. Animals were live-trapped, equipped with a GPS transmitter, and released. For each tagged individual, the researchers recorded the sex, age, personality (based on behavior in the trap), and an index for the abundance of reindeer in the area used by the animal. They then recorded whether the animal was still alive after 1 year of monitoring.

            "MASS",   # AIC
            "nimble", # model fitting Bayesian example
            "coda"    # post-processing, used w nimble
)
# Call the libraries
sapply(lbs, library, char = TRUE)

# Specify path and load data
url_remote <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
path_git   <- "MTourani/WILD541_F2026/refs/heads/main/"
load(url(paste0(url_remote, path_git, "weasel.RData")))
head(weasel)


As always, inspect the data, tally the information, and visualize the different variables before model fitting.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab

Full model
Our goal is to determine which variables influence survival and how. Based on our knowledge of the system, we build the most complex model that we are willing to consider. In this case, we allow only 2-way interactions.









Looking at the model output, you notice that several of the coefficients estimated by the model are not significantly different from 0. Apparently, this model uses too many parameters that do not seem to explain the variation in these data.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Step-wise selection based on parsimony
With AIC-based model selection, the goal is to find the model (or group of models) with the lowest AIC-value(s). The absolute value itself is not important.

Note also, that you can only use AIC to compare models fitted to the same data set!

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Step-wise selection based on parsimony
We can use the stepAIC() function in the MASS library to do a step-wise selection of terms, shown next.
In each step, the function removes the term whose removal results in the lowest AIC value. Once no more terms can be removed without a reduction in AIC, the procedure stops and returns the top model.









You could display the terms included in the top model and check the output of the top model using summary() and formula().

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
A-priori candidate models: frequentist
A drawback of the step-wise selection process is that, due to the sequential removal (or addition) of terms, a predictor may be dropped from a more complex model when it is actually important in the simpler model. As an alternative to the step-wise selection procedure, you can build multiple candidate models and then compare these using AIC (or WAIC in the next example).









Based on the results, which model is superior (lowest AIC) to the other three models in this comparison?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Setup: load data
If you saved “.RData” in your RStudio project folder last week, you can load it as below. It’s a good practice to start by emptying the workspace and then loading the data.

rm(list = ls())            # Clear workspace
load("snapshot_usa.RData") # Load data


Otherwise, you can load the original “.csv”:

rm(list = ls())  # Clear workspace

library(utils)   # Load required R package

# Specify data path
url_remote <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
path_git   <- "MTourani/WILD541_F2026/refs/heads/main/"

# Load data
snapshot_usa <- utils::read.csv(paste0(url_remote, path_git, "snapshot_usa.csv"))

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Data preparation: new column
Let’s add a column so that every row has a unique ID.

# Add unique row ID
snapshot_usa$ID <- seq_len(nrow(snapshot_usa))

Next, let’s extract the week number and add it as a new column to the existing table:

# Extract numeric week number (handles "2019-W35" format)
snapshot_usa$Week <- as.integer(sub(".*-W(\\d+).*",
                                    "\\1",
                                    snapshot_usa$Week,
                                    perl = TRUE)
)

# Inspect the table
head(snapshot_usa)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Data preparation: subset
As you learned in the previous class, we can use conditions to subset data. For example, we could ask how many mammal species were recorded at least once.

mammal_snapshot <- snapshot_usa[snapshot_usa$Class == "Mammals", ]
# Number of mammal species
length(unique(mammal_snapshot$Species_Name))

# Number of days with at least one photo

# Number of deployment locations with at least one photo



How many survey days have at least one photo? How many deployment locations?

text:
Data preparation: aggregate
Let’s aggregate and find the number of observations per animal class or species.

# How many observations per animal class?
aggregate(ID ~ Class,
          data = snapshot_usa,
          FUN  = function(x)length(unique(x)))



Can you find the species with the most number of detection locations?


# How many detection locations per species?
aggregate(Deployment_ID ~ Species_Name,
          data = snapshot_usa,
          FUN = function(x)length(unique(x)))

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Data preparation: aggregate

# Observations per week
tab1 <- aggregate(ID ~ Week,
                  data = snapshot_usa,
                  FUN  = function(x) length(unique(x)))

# Per species per week
tab2 <- aggregate(ID ~ Common_Name + Week,
                  data = snapshot_usa,
                  FUN  = function(x) length(unique(x)))

# Per class per week
tab3 <- aggregate(ID ~ Class + Week,
                  data = snapshot_usa,
                  FUN  = function(x) length(unique(x)))

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Simple plot
The plot() function is the basic function for generating plots in R.

plot(snapshot_usa$ID ~ snapshot_usa$Week)


The formula y∼x indicates to plot() that time (week) should be plotted on the x-axis as a function of the number of IDs on the y-axis.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Simple plot
We could also use aggregated tables for plotting to make more sense of the data.

plot(tab1$ID ~ tab1$Week)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Customize a plot
Within the plot() function, you have a lot of options to customize the graph. See the examples below.

plot(tab1$ID ~ tab1$Week,
     xlab  = "Week",
     ylab  = "Number of photos",
     type  = "l",
     lty   = 2,
     col   = "grey",
     axes  = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1),
     ylim  = c(min(tab1$ID)  - 30, max(tab1$ID)  + 200),
     lwd   = 2, 
     xaxs  = "i", 
     yaxs  = "i", 
     frame = FALSE)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Customizing the axes
The default axes produced by plot() are often appropriate, but sometimes we want to have more control over the axes, including their position and scale. To create custom axes, set the axes argument in the plot() function to FALSE and then execute a separate axis() function for each axis.

plot(tab1$ID ~ tab1$Week,
     type  = "l",
     lty   = 2,
     col   = "grey", 
     axes  = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1),
     ylim  = c(min(tab1$ID) - 30,  max(tab1$ID) + 200),
     lwd   = 2,
     xaxs  = "i", 
     yaxs  = "i",
     frame = FALSE,
     xlab  = "Week",
     ylab  = "Number of photos")
 
axis(1,
     at    = seq(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1, 2),
     label = seq(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1, 2),
     las   = 1,
     lwd   = 2)


Which axis was just added to the plot?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Customizing the axes
Similarly, add the second axis as shown below.

plot(tab1$ID ~ tab1$Week,
     type  = "l",
     lty   = 2,
     col   = "grey", 
     axes  = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1),
     ylim  = c(0, max(tab1$ID) + 200),
     lwd   = 2,
     xaxs  = "i", 
     yaxs  = "i", 
     frame = FALSE,
     xlab  = "Week",
     ylab  = "Number of photos")

axis(1,
     at = seq(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1, 2),
     label = seq(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1, 2),
     las = 1, 
     lwd = 2)
axis(2,
     at = seq(0, max(tab1$ID), 200),
     label = seq(0, max(tab1$ID), 200), 
     las = 1, lwd = 2)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Customizing the plot
Finally, add the points to the already existing plot.

plot(tab1$ID ~ tab1$Week,
     type  = "l",
     lty   = 2,
     col   = "grey", 
     axes  = FALSE,
     xlim  = c(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1),
     ylim  = c(0, max(tab1$ID) + 200),
     lwd   = 2,
     xaxs  = "i", 
     yaxs  = "i", 
     frame = FALSE,
     xlab  = "Week",
     ylab  = "Number of photos")

axis(1,
     at = seq(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1, 2),
     label = seq(min(tab1$Week) - 1, max(tab1$Week) + 1, 2),
     las = 1, 
     lwd = 2)
axis(2,
     at = seq(0, max(tab1$ID), 200),
     label = seq(0, max(tab1$ID), 200), 
     las = 1, lwd = 2)

points(tab1$ID ~ tab1$Week, pch = 21, bg = "firebrick", cex = 1.1)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Conveying additional information
We can use plots for a graphical comparison between two groups. For example, we can plot the number of bird observations vs mammals’. We first plot the number of mammal records per survey week, and then add to the existing plot the number of bird records.

tab3_mammals <- tab3[tab3$Class == "Mammals", ]
tab3_aves    <- tab3[tab3$Class == "Aves",    ]

plot(tab3_mammals$ID ~ tab3_mammals$Week,
     col  = "orange",
     lwd  = 3,
     pch  = 19,
     xlab = "Week",
     ylab = "Number of photos",
     main = "")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Conveying additional information
You can enrich the data part of your graphs by adding additional features such as colors, text, etc. This allows you to convey more information than just the usual 2 dimensions.

plot(tab3_mammals$ID ~ tab3_mammals$Week,
     col  = "orange",
     lwd  = 3,
     pch  = 19,
     xlab = "Week",
     ylab = "Number of photos",
     main = "")

points(tab3_aves$ID ~ tab3_aves$Week,
       pch = 17,
       col = "lightblue", 
       lwd = 3)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Aves", "Mammals"),
       lwd    = 3, 
       pch    = c(17, 19),
       col    = c("lightblue", "orange"))

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Barplot
Let’s use a barplot to display the number of records for canids.

canid_index <- c("Coyote",
                 "Domestic Dog",
                 "Red Fox",
                 "Gray Fox",
                 "Gray Wolf",
                 "Kit Fox",
                 "Red Wolf")
canid_snapshot <- mammal_snapshot[mammal_snapshot$Common_Name %in% canid_index, ]
mx <- table(canid_snapshot$Common_Name)

barplot(height    = mx,
        xlab      = "Canid species",
        ylab      = "Number of photos",
        names.arg = names(mx),
        density   = seq(10, 70, 10),
        col       = "firebrick")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Stacked barplot
How about the number of records per week for bears?

bear_index <- c("Ursus arctos", "Ursus americanus")
bear <- mammal_snapshot[mammal_snapshot$Species_Name %in% bear_index, ]
mx   <- table(bear$Species_Name, bear$Week)

barplot(height    = mx, 
        width     = 10,
        xlab      = "Week",
        ylab      = "Number of photos",
        names.arg = colnames(mx),
        beside    = TRUE,
        density   = c(20, 50), 
        col       = "black")
legend(210,
       100,
       legend  = unique(bear$Species_Name),
       density = c(20, 50),
       bty     = "n", 
       title   = "")

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
section: Add text labels to a plot
text:
Add text labels to a plot
You can add text (e.g., point labels) inside a plot. Let’s plot the weekly number of records per species (tab2) and flag the species with the most weekly records. One approach is to first use order() and see which species have over 1000 detections per week.

tab4 <- tab2[order(tab2$ID, decreasing = TRUE), ]

plot(tab4$ID ~ tab4$Week,
     xlab = "Week",
     ylab = "Number of photos",
     ylim = c(0, max(tab4$ID) + 120))

text(tab4$ID[1:9] ~ tab4$Week[1:9],
     labels = tab4$Common_Name[1:9],
     pos    = 1, 
     cex    = 0.7)

# Highlight top records in colour
points(tab4$ID[1:9] ~ tab4$Week[1:9], col = "turquoise")


In the above plot, we have flagged the highest number of weekly records by adding the species name. Now, can you use colors to flag these points?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Customizing the plot
Let’s filter tab2 and keep canids and display the number of weekly records per canid species. You can pick one color for each input type from the color scale provided by function topo.colors().

tab5     <- tab2[tab2$Common_Name %in% canid_index, ]
my_cols  <- topo.colors(length(unique(tab5$Common_Name)))
names(my_cols) <- unique(tab5$Common_Name)

plot(ID ~ Week, 
     data = tab5,
     ylab = "Number of photos",
     xlab = "Week",
     xlim = c(min(tab5$Week) - 1, max(tab5$Week) + 3),
     pch = 19,
     col = my_cols[Common_Name],
     cex = 1.3, 
     main = "")

legend("topright",
       legend = unique(tab5$Common_Name),
       pch    = 19,
       cex    = 1, 
       pt.cex = 1.5, 
       col    = my_cols)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Multiple panels
Often, we display multiple graphs in multiple panels as part of the same figure. You can use the par() function to split your display into panels. In the previous table, let’s filter foxes and make one plot per fox species.

tab6     <- tab5[grep("Fox", tab5$Common_Name), ]
my_cols  <- c("darkorange", "grey", "lightblue")
names(my_cols) <- unique(tab6$Common_Name)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (i in seq_along(unique(tab6$Common_Name))) {
  this_fox <- unique(tab6$Common_Name)[i]
  plot(ID ~ Week,
       data = tab6[tab6$Common_Name == this_fox, ],
       ylab = "Number of photos",
       xlab = "Week",
       xlim = c(min(tab6$Week) - 1, max(tab6$Week) + 3),
       ylim = c(0, max(tab6$ID) + 3),
       pch = 19, 
       cex = 1.3,
       col = my_cols[Common_Name],
       type = "h",
       lend = 1, 
       lwd = 5,
       main = this_fox)
}
par(mfrow = c(1,1))

Plot device

windows(4,4)
plot(ID ~ Week,
     data = tab6[tab6$Common_Name == "Red Fox",],
     ylab = "Number of photos",
     xlab = "Week",
     xlim = c(min(tab6$Week) - 1, max(tab6$Week) + 3),
     ylim = c(0, max(tab6$ID) + 3),
     pch  = 19,
     col  = my_cols[Common_Name],
     cex  = 1.3, 
     type = "h",
     lend = 1,
     lwd = 5,

)







tip



You can open a new plot window, outside of R, with the windows() function. This can be helpful if you want to have multiple plots open simultaneously for comparison or if you want to see what your plot looks like given a certain size and aspect ratio.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Plot device
We want to make it easy for the viewer to pick out the important relationships or differences in our figure. Aside from the features mentioned earlier in this lesson, you can control the appearance of a plot and thus the emphasis on its characteristics by changing the scaling of the axes and their aspect ratio. To see how important the choice of aspect can be, run the following code and then resize the plot window by stretching it out horizontally.

x <- seq(1, 100, 0.5)
y <- sin(x)
windows(5, 3)
plot(y ~ x)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab

Exporting figures

Here we specify the attributes of the figure.

tiff(filename = "myplot.tif", width = 10, height = 7, units = "cm", res = 300)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Measuring probability

What is the probability of trout being captured by an osprey?



The event is a predator attack.
An attack has 2 outcomes: escape or capture.
These outcomes are discrete.
The set {(escape), (capture)} consisting of all the possibles outcomes is called the sample space.
We are interested in the outcome «capture».
Each attack is also called a trial.
A set of trials is an experiment.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Simulating data
One way to understand distributions is to generate and inspect simulated data.
Simulated data from a known distribution can also be compared with real data to identify which distribution the data came from.
Here you will learn how to simulate data from common theoretical distributions, as well as how to visualize and compare them.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Uniform distribution
Let’s start with 100 draws from a uniform distribution between 0 and 10.

x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)

We can summarize the resulting data:

summary(x_unif)

… and plot the raw data in the order in which the samples were drawn:

plot(x_unif, type = "h")


Compare your simulated data with your neighbor. Did you generate the same values?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Uniform distribution
You can use set.seed() to make your simulation reproducible.

set.seed(2026)
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)
summary(x_unif)
plot(x_unif, type = "h")


Compare your simulated data with your neighbor. Did you generate the same values?

set.seed(2026)
x_unif <- runif(n = 100, min = 0, max = 10)
hist(x_unif)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Normal distribution
We can draw samples from a normal distribution using function rnorm(). We provide the number of samples to be drawn, the mean, and the standard deviation.

x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)
summary(x_norm)
plot(x_norm, type = "h")


Are the sample mean and standard deviation identical to the specified values?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Visualization
The previous plot gives us an idea about the spread (apparently symmetrical around 0) and order (random) of values, but it is not a great way to discern their distribution. There are different ways to visualize the distribution. We can, for example, use a histogram:

set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)
hist(x_norm)

or a Kernel density plot, with vertical lines added for the mean and 95% confidence interval:

set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)
plot(density(x_norm))
abline(v = mean(x_norm), lwd = 2, col = "red")
ci <- quantile(x_norm, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
abline(v = ci, col = "red", lty = 2)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Visualization
We can also plot a Kernel density on top of the histogram:

set.seed(2026)
x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)
hist(x_norm, probability = TRUE)
lines(density(x_norm), col = "red", lwd = 4)







Note



Here we display the probability, instead of the frequency of falling into a bin of values. This allows us to compare the histogram and density kernel in the same plot.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Visualization
We can compare two distributions by plotting their Kernel densities in the same graph:

set.seed(2026)
x1_norm <- rnorm(1000, mean = 25, sd = 5)
x2_norm <- rnorm(1000, mean = 15, sd = 2)

plot(density(x1_norm), col = "red",  lwd = 4, ylim = c(0, 0.30))
lines(density(x2_norm), col = "blue", lwd = 4)

or by plotting them as box-and-whisker plots:

set.seed(2026)
x1_norm <- rnorm(1000, mean = 25, sd = 5)
x2_norm <- rnorm(1000, mean = 15, sd = 2)

data1  <- data.frame(x = x1_norm, sample = "A")
data2  <- data.frame(x = x2_norm, sample = "B")
my_data <- rbind(data1, data2)

boxplot(x ~ sample, data = my_data)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Poisson distribution
Count data are often assumed to follow a Poisson distribution. You can simulate count data using the rpois() function. As you recall the normal distribution has two parameters, the mean and the standard deviation. The Poisson function only has one parameter, the mean count λ (lambda). Here is an example of how to generate and display Poisson data:

x_pois <- rpois(n = 250, lambda = 3.3)
hist(x_pois, probability = TRUE)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Poisson distribution
Here too, we can compare the distribution of different samples in the same plot:

x1_pois <- rpois(250, lambda = 3.3)
x2_pois <- rpois(250, lambda = 1.5)
max_count <- max(c(x1_pois, x2_pois))

hist(x1_pois,
     probability = TRUE,
     breaks = 0 : max_count,
     ylim = c(0, 0.8),
     xlab = "x",
     main = "")
hist(x2_pois,
     add = TRUE, 
     probability = TRUE,
     col = adjustcolor("blue", 0.25),
     border = "blue",
     breaks = 0 : max_count)

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Binomial distribution
The binomial distribution results from a process whereby repeated trials lead to either success or failure. In R, we can use the rbinom() function, which takes as arguments the sample size (number of observations), the number of trials per observation, and the probability of success in a given trial. In the following example, we draw 10 samples from a Binomial distribution based on 5 trials and a 0.25 probability of success:

x_binom <- rbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.25)



The output gives the number of successes (out of 5 trials) for each of the 10 samples we drew.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Bernoulli distribution
The Bernoulli distribution is a special case of the Binomial distribution where each observation consists of only a single trial. For example, we can draw 10 samples from a Bernoulli distribution using the rbinom() function like this:

# e.g., flipping a coin with P(heads) = 0.35
x_bern <- rbinom(n = 10, size = 1, prob = 0.35)


This is essentially the same as tossing a coin 10 times. In this example, the probability of getting heads (“success”) instead of tails (“failure”) is 0.35.

One way to display the distribution of the resulting data is as a bar plot of the tabulated results, showing the frequency of a success vs. failure:

barplot(table(x_bern == 1),
        xlab = "Outcome",
        ylab = "Number of cases")

Why use GLM?
A linear model describes the relationship between a response and explanatory variable(s), assuming:



The model makes biological sense
Independence of errors (blocking, mixed effects models later)
Homoscedasticity — equal variance of errors
Normality of errors

\[y = b_0   \times X_0 + b_1    \times X_1 + b_2    \times X_2 + \ldots\]

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
What is a GLM?
In a Gaussian linear model, the expected values are:


\[\mu = X \beta\]
and the errors follow a normal distribution:
\[y \sim    {Normal}(\mu, \sigma)\]






Note


But are the errors always normal? What if our response is a count, a proportion, or presence/absence?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Model structure
Statistical models describe:

Systematic pattern in a random variable (response), possibly as a function of covariates
Random (unexplained) variability around the mean:

Response = systematic + random






Note


other pairs of terms: deterministic + stochastic, or mean + dispersion structure of model

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Key elements of a model


Deterministic process:


Stochastic process:



Why do we need both? Deterministic part is a mathematical model of a process while stochastic part is a statistical model of data that arise from the process.

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Basic regression model
Deterministic process: What biological process underlies the pattern in my data?
Stochastic process: What probabilistic process produces the values of my data?
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \sim  {Normal}(0, \sigma^2)\]
is exactly the same as:
\[\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \qquad y_i \sim    {Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma^2)\]

What if the errors aren’t normal?

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Common error distributions






The family for the errors can be: Gaussian for normally distributed data

Other example error distributions include:


Poisson for count data
Binomial for success/failure data
Bernoulli for presence/absence

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
What is a GLM?
A GLM uses a link function \(L\) to describe the relationship between the mean response and the predictor:
\[L(E(y)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]

title: WILD 541 – Research Design Lab
text:
Simple linear regression
\[E(y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... + \beta_n x_n\]

The link is called ”identity”
Produces μ on range (−∞, ∞)
Possibility to add interaction effects (e.g., \(\beta_3 x_1 x_2\)) and curvilinear effects (e.g., \(\beta_4 x_1^3\) )
When should we not use a linear model?
– Simple linear models produce continuous predictions across the range of all real numbers
– Equations must provide predictions matched to the biological quantities we wish to understand

Relationships with count data as the response can be modeled using Poisson GLM. A logarithmic link is used between the expectation of the response (i.e., the mean count) and the predictor function (i.e., the combination of parameters on the right side of the regression equation). As a result, exponentiated coefficient estimates are the multiplicative effect on the count (response) of one unit increase in the predictor.
